newsitem.title: USA: Air Force reopens probe of fiery N.C. crash.
newsitem.headline: Air Force reopens probe of fiery N.C. crash.

text.p: On orders from the Pentagon's inspector general, the Air Force said on Friday it will reopen its investigation of a fiery 1994 aircraft collision in North Carolina that killed 23 U.S. soldiers.

The service earlier ruled that errors by civilian and military air traffic controllers were chiefly responsible for the mid-air collision of an F-16 fighter jet and a C-130 cargo plane at Pope Air Force Base near Fort Bragg, sparking one of the worst U.S. military peacetime disasters.

The damaged F-16 slammed into a runway parking ramp after its two crewmen ejected safely, spewing flaming wreckage into paratroopers waiting to board a C-141 transport. Twenty-three soldiers died and nearly 100 were injured on March 23, 1994.

The Air Force said on Friday that the Pentagon's inspector general, in a review of the investigation, did not question the fault of controllers but asked that the actions of F-16 pilot Capt. Joseph Jacyno be further investigated.
Jacyno was subsequently assigned to Moody AFB near Valdosta, Ga., Air Force officials said on Friday.
"The (inspector general's) report concluded the aircraft accident investigation report failed to adequately assess the actions of the F-16 pilot..." the Air Force said.
It said Air Force Secretary Sheila Widnall directed a reopening of the investigation "to reassess the actions of the F-16 pilot in light of the findings in the report."
The F-16 was badly damaged in its collision with the C-130 as both were trying to land at the same time at Pope. The C-130 landed safely despite damage caused in the crash.

Air Force officials declined to comment publicly on the new investigation, but one said privately it could look into whether the fighter pilot should have seen the C-130 and tried to avoid it despite an OK to land from a civilian air traffic controller in North Carolina.

The Air Force said the Pentagon's inspector general ruled that the service did not cover up any evidence and gave no indication that disciplinary action taken against military flight controllers was incorrect.
"The accident investigation findings, conclusions and recommendations relating to air trffic control failures were supported by the evidence," the Air Force said.
